hook: You know the verse about grace, not works. But did you know the letter carries the name of a city that once chanted for two hours to defend its goddess?
story:
Picture the city before you picture the verse.

Ephesus sat on the west coast of what is now Turkey, and its goddess was Artemis. Her great temple was the city's pride, and the city's living: a silversmith named Demetrius “made silver shrines of Artemis” and “brought no little business to the craftsmen”. Then Paul spent years among them. Luke says “the word of the Lord was growing and becoming mighty.” Many who had practiced magical arts “brought their books together and burned them in the sight of all.” They counted the price: “fifty thousand pieces of silver.”

Then the trade felt the loss. Demetrius gathered the workmen and warned that “the temple of the great goddess Artemis will be counted as nothing”. The crowd “were filled with anger,” and “The whole city was filled with confusion”. They rushed into the theater. Luke adds that “Most of them didn’t know why they had come together”, and for about two hours they cried out, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”

This is the city whose name the letter carries. It was a place where worth was something you built, bought and defended, with temples, with trade, with the right gods. Into that world comes a sentence that says what matters most cannot be built or bought: “for by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works, that no one would boast.”

voices.name: John Wesley
voices.about: Anglican priest, opening a sermon on this verse at St. Mary’s, Oxford, on 18 June 1738
voices.words: All the blessings which God hath bestowed upon man are of his mere grace, bounty, or favour; his free, undeserved favour; favour altogether undeserved; man having no claim to the least of his mercies.

moment:
The verse sits in the middle of a sentence that begins with a grim picture. The readers “were dead in transgressions and sins,” and then comes the turn: “But God, being rich in mercy” and he “made us alive together with Christ”. Verses 8 and 9 explain how that happened: it was grace, received through faith, and a gift. Verse 10 then says what the gift is for: “we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works”. The works are not missing from the letter. They come after the gift, not before it.

The letter names Paul as its writer, and near its end he calls himself “an ambassador in chains”. Tradition places that in a Roman prison. Earlier, when Paul left the region, the elders of the church “all wept freely, and fell on Paul’s neck and kissed him, sorrowing most of all because of the word which he had spoken, that they should see his face no more.”
around: Right after the verse, the letter turns to the other side of the same truth. Those who were once “separate from Christ” and “strangers from the covenants of the promise” are now “made near”. He “broke down the middle wall of separation,” and “you are no longer strangers and foreigners, but you are fellow citizens with the saints”. Grace is not only about a person standing before God alone. It also gathers people who used to stand on opposite sides.
after:
The Bible tells us more about Ephesus. In Acts, Paul calls the elders of the church to Miletus and reminds them that he served “with many tears”. They “wept freely” and went with him to the ship. In the book of Revelation, the church at Ephesus is praised for its “perseverance” and for testing false apostles, and then comes the line: “But I have this against you, that you left your first love.” It is a warning, and it also tells them what to do: “Remember therefore from where you have fallen, and repent”.

The city itself did not last. The 1911 Britannica says the Goths destroyed both city and temple in A.D. 262. A general council of the Church met there in 431. Livius says its decline began when the harbor silted up, and the 1911 Britannica adds that the city was gradually deserted owing to its malaria. The temple Demetrius feared for is gone, and the letter sent to the city is still read.

Centuries later, Augustine and Wesley both went back to this verse.
readings:
Readers have taken the verse in several ways, and they often agree on more than they think.

One reading, Augustine’s, presses on the word “gift”. He understood the gift to include faith itself, so that nobody could say that believing was their own achievement. Another reading hears the verse as a plain statement that everything God gives is undeserved, from the first breath to the last, as John Wesley said in the sermon he preached on it. A third looks at the letter around the verse. Some scholars say its central concern is the unity of Jewish and Gentile believers, and on that reading “no one would boast” is also about two groups who could each have boasted over the other.

A further question is about the letter itself. Many scholars question whether Paul wrote it, and the words “in Ephesus” are missing from some early manuscripts, which is why many think it was a letter meant to travel among several churches. Neither point changes what the verse says. It changes only what we know about how it first traveled.
argued:
Augustine of Hippo took up the verse in his book On Grace and Free Will, against the thought that people might claim credit for their own faith. He pointed out that the verse says the faith is a gift too, and that the works the next verse speaks of are not set aside: [[augustine]]

Centuries later, John Wesley chose the verse as the text for a sermon preached at St. Mary’s, Oxford, before the University, and began with the width of grace: [[wesley]] Two men from very different centuries went back to the same verse.
point: Read alone, the verse is a famous summary of grace. Read in Ephesus, it is a word to people who knew what it was to work, trade and defend what they had. The letter tells them that the thing at the center of their new life was given, and that the good works come after the gift, as verse 10 says, not before.
lesson:
The people of Ephesus knew the cost of everything. Most of us do too: we know what it takes to be respected, to be safe, to be good enough. The verse says that with God, you are not asked to pay for the one thing that matters most.

That can be hard to hear if you have spent your life earning. It can sound too easy, or like an insult to everything you have done. Notice what the letter does not say. It does not say your effort is worthless. Verse 10 says there are good works prepared for you. The order is the point: you start from the gift, and you do not work to get to it.

If you carry a feeling that you have not done enough, you could read Ephesians 2 slowly, from the start to verse 10, and see where it begins. If you do not share this faith, the passage still says something clear about the people who first read it: that what they were given was not what they had earned.

echoes.note: In another letter attributed to Paul, salvation comes “not by works of righteousness which we did ourselves, but according to his mercy”. The same truth, in a letter to a church on Crete.
Paul asks, “Where then is the boasting? It is excluded.” It is the same point as the end of Ephesians 2:9, said to a church in Rome.
“And if by grace, then it is no longer of works; otherwise grace is no longer grace.” Here Paul shows why grace and earning cannot be mixed.
